title: Examining his Buffet clarinet; keys and reeds
summary: Looking at his Buffet Albert system clarinet, its keys, his third California instrument and his reed strengths.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Well, you were showing us your clarinet. Yeah.
And you look through it in the light, the bore that drilled the hole in there, see how big that hole. Oh, yeah, it's really a big bore. Well, it's much bigger than the buffet.
What make is this?
That's a buffet. This is it.
This is it.
Yeah, it was the medical system. Do you see the difference, Mr. Roussel? The road hand on the bell. Do you see the difference in that,

Liz Buffett and my Buffett? I don't know. No, I don't remember. Why? I don't know. I've never had yours in my hand very much. Once you see it, it's all right. Does this have more keys than yours? No, I say oh my. Do you see it? No. It's straight, a little piece like a... Oh, sure, yeah.
Why didn't I see that? Yeah. The minus giants in that. It doesn't come apart yet. Keep it all in one long piece. Yeah, the case is like a violin case.
Yeah. Raymond Burke has one like that,
both an A and a B-flat, all in one piece. Big long case.
Yeah, I never even said it. That's improved.
It must be improved. I've never made them like that before. Three keys down here.
Yeah, look at your... Yeah, that key feels like it's up sort of high though, do you think? Oh, so you have it up there then? Yeah, that's right. Yeah.

About stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff like stuff like stuff stuff like stuff stuff Well, I don't have to use the others.
You don't have to use a bunch anyway.
No, just use that big one for C-sharp. And that other one on the outside of C-sharp, the E-flat, I never have to go over there for it.
Is this the same instrument you had in the Army and carried all that time?
No, I just told him that's the third one I had in California.
Third one you got out there.
Yeah.
Yeah, I guess you call that an improved, Albert.

It was improved for the ones I had. It didn't have no keys or no rolls or nothing. But I always used a buffet because that's what Papa Teal had. The clarinet players there, if you didn't have a buffet, you didn't have no clarinet.

What kind of fest has gotten? You say George Barquet got yours fest for you? Yeah, Malcolm, Alfred Wilson. Oh, yeah, piano player. I'm always going to ask what kind of a reed you use. Do you use a stiff reed or medium or soft? What kind of a reed do you like?

Well, since I don't play so often, I use a number three. They call that almost medium. Yeah, number three. And then when I play band music, I have what they call a plastic reed. It's a number four. It don't become water soap. It changes the tone. You don't get a sweeter tone or a soft tone like you would. So playing street music, you want to hear the clarinet. And most of the clarinet players around here, they're used to sitting down and play, and they can't walk in place. So I try to help out. But I play strong. But other than that, I use a number three.
